forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Gedling forecasts internal borrowing at 49% of borrowing need, against approved indicator of 45%
news_drafts.lead:
Gedling Borough Council expects to pay for 49% of its underlying need to borrow from its own cash rather than from loans, above the 45% it has approved as its indicator for the year. The figure is in a report to Cabinet on 15 October covering treasury activity from April to July 2026 and the council's prudential indicators, the limits and measures every council must publish to show its borrowing is affordable.

The practice is called internal borrowing: using the council's own reserves, money it has put aside, to pay for capital spending on things that last, such as buildings, roads, vehicles and equipment. It saves interest but uses up the cushion. The percentage is measured against the council's capital financing requirement, the total it has spent on long-lived assets and not yet paid for.

The projection has risen from 45% in the 2026/27 budget. The report calls it "a temporary fluctuation due to last years slippage of the capital programme", the council's planned capital spending. It says the figure is "expected to be back in line later in the year as schemes from the current year are rephased".
news_drafts.paper_title: Prudential Code Indicator Monitoring 2026/27 and Treasury Activity Report for the Period April 2026 to July 2026

news_drafts.headline: Gedling's waste, street care and fleet services ended 2025/26 £820,197 over original budget
news_drafts.lead:
Gedling Council's waste, street care and transport and fleet services spent £820,197, or 21%, more than their original budget in 2025/26. The figure comes from the year's outturn (the actual figures once the year has ended), reported to Cabinet on 25 June. Against the revised budget approved during the year, the overspend was £333,681. The council's General Fund, which pays for day-to-day running costs, finished the year £1.3m underspent overall.

The papers put the pressure down mainly to staffing and agency costs, driven by sickness absence and recruitment difficulties. The variance analysis lists waste residual £114,000 over, fleet management £207,000 and street care £16,000. It cites "additional agency, hire of vehicles, parts and repairs and external servicing and repairs". Corporate Management was £165,000 over, "mainly due to increased staffing costs". For 2026/27 the council is optimising its waste management system to improve efficiency. The papers do not yet show whether it will work.

Separately, bids for replacing fire doors came in above the £125,900 approved budget. An extra £27,400 was needed for "essential H&S compliance works", met from unspent Asset Management Fund budget. The council has asked to carry forward £153,300 (move unspent money into the next year) for the project.

findings.paper_title: Budget Virement Report and Performance monitoring for the period April to July 2026
findings.headline: Annual Delivery Plan 92.3% on track: 48 of 52 expected milestones completed in the first four-month period.
findings.detail: The council has achieved 92.3% milestone completion in the first period. Achievements include delivery of the Arnold Summer Fair, maintaining Green Flag status for parks, progress on the draft Local Plan, preparation for Renters' Rights implementation, waste and depot modernisation milestones, decommissioning of the Richard Herrod Centre, and strategic asset management progress.
findings.matters: Maintaining high strategic delivery momentum despite financial pressures and performance issues indicates effective prioritisation and management of competing demands.
findings.quote: At Period 1, 48 of 52 expected milestones have been completed, representing a completion rate of 92.3%.

findings.paper_title: Budget Virement Report and Performance monitoring for the period April to July 2026
findings.headline: Housing delivery 181 homes vs 212 target; affordable housing 19 delivered vs 37 target.
findings.detail: The council is 14.6% below target on net additional homes (181 vs 212). Affordable housing delivery is particularly low at 19 units against a target of 37, 48.6% below target. The council is developing the Local Development Plan to allocate sites to meet the borough's revised housing requirement.
findings.matters: Housing delivery affects the council's Council Tax base growth assumptions and local economic development strategy. Shortfalls, particularly in affordable housing, may indicate viability or capacity issues.
findings.figures: Net additional homes 181 vs 212 target; affordable homes 19 vs 37 target

findings.paper_title: Budget Virement Report and Performance monitoring for the period April to July 2026
findings.headline: Complaint volumes increased to 471 in the period, 307 more than in the previous four-month period.
findings.detail: Complaints rose from 164 in the previous four-month period to 471, a 187% increase. Complaints peaked in May and June, reflecting changes to garden waste collection rounds, reducing in July and August as arrangements became established. Only 64% of complaints were processed within the required timescale, down 10 percentage points from the previous period.
findings.matters: Sharp increases in complaint volumes indicate service disruption or customer dissatisfaction, creating additional officer time for investigation, escalation and corrective action.
findings.figures: 471 complaints vs 164 in previous period (307 additional, 187% increase); 64% processed within timescale
findings.quote: The Council received 471 complaints in total, 307 more than in the previous four-month period.

findings.paper_title: Budget Virement Report and Performance monitoring for the period April to July 2026
findings.headline: Customer service response time performance at 61.5% within SLA vs 85% target; benefits processing taking 25 days vs 15 day target.
findings.detail: Customer service performance has deteriorated, with only 61.5% of calls answered within the 40-second SLA (target 85%). Benefits processing is delayed at 25 days vs 15-day target. Both issues are linked to operational capacity and transformation activity, with the wider measure of calls answered or receiving a call-back remaining above target.
findings.matters: Performance deterioration in customer-facing services indicates resource constraints or capacity issues, which can drive complaints, escalations, and additional officer time.
findings.figures: Customer service 61.5% vs 85% target; benefits processing 25 days vs 15 day target
findings.quote: LI5002 Percentage of Calls to customer service answered within SLA (40 seconds) 61.5% 85%

findings.paper_title: Budget Virement Report and Performance monitoring for the period April to July 2026
findings.headline: Business Rates collection at 38.42% vs 37.12% target; collection rates outperforming alongside strong performance in related areas.
findings.detail: Business Rates collection is outperforming the target by 1.3 percentage points. Strong collection performance improves cashflow timing and the level of cash balances available for investment, supporting treasury management alongside the strong performance in invoices paid within 30 days (99.26%), planning application processing, and private-sector housing interventions.
findings.matters: Collection rate performance directly affects the council's cash position and treasury management. Collection outperformance provides positive cashflow management and working capital support.

daily_post.headline: Entire borrowing portfolio concentrated in long-term: 94% over 10 years, zero borrowing under 5 years
daily_post.lead: Lenders assess maturity profile to evaluate refinancing risk; a portfolio with no short-term buffer and nearly all debt over 10 years creates a refinancing cliff when those loans mature, with no diversification across maturity dates to spread the risk
